hints: Compare the functional groups in G, which has $\text{CHO}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, with the product $\text{HOOC(CH}_2)_2\text{COOH}$ and think about gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen.
walkthrough:
Track what changes in the functional groups**
Look closely at G, $\text{OHCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. It has an aldehyde at one end and a primary alcohol at the other. The product is $\text{HOOC(CH}_2)_2\text{COOH}$, a dioic acid. Both ends have gained oxygen and lost hydrogen, which is the classic signature of oxidation in organic chemistry.

hints: Recall which strong oxidising agent converts both a primary alcohol and an aldehyde all the way to carboxylic acids.
Think about the acid and heating conditions needed to keep the oxidiser working and to prevent volatile aldehyde escaping before full oxidation.
walkthrough:
Choose the strong oxidiser**
To push $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ to $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{CHO}$ to $\text{COOH}$ you need a powerful oxidiser. Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, does exactly this.

Add the conditions for complete oxidation**
Acid is essential to provide $\text{H}^+$ for the dichromate half equation, and heating under reflux returns any volatile intermediate to the flask so oxidation goes to completion with no loss of aldehyde.
Final answer: acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$; heat under reflux

hints: Remember that Na reacts with the acidic $\text{O-H}$ of an alcohol to release $\text{H}_2$, but leaves an aldehyde $\text{C=O}$ untouched.
walkthrough:
Let only the alcohol react**
Picture G meeting Na. The $\text{-OH}$ proton is acidic enough to react: $2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_2$. The aldehyde group $\text{-CHO}$ has no acidic $\text{O-H}$ so it survives unchanged. You get the sodium alkoxide with the aldehyde intact, $\text{OHCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{ONa}$.
Final answer: $\text{OHCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{ONa}$ or $\text{OHC(CH}_2)_3\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$

hints: Recall what happens when Tollens' reagent, ammoniacal silver nitrate, oxidises an aldehyde and itself gets reduced to metallic silver.
walkthrough:
Visualise the Tollens' positive result**
Tollens' reagent contains $\text{[Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$. An aldehyde like G reduces it to metallic $\text{Ag}$, while the aldehyde is oxidised to a carboxylate. The silver coats the inside of the clean test tube as a shiny silver mirror.
Final answer: silver mirror / grey precipitate of silver forms

hints: Notice reaction 4 joins a $\text{COOH}$ and an $\text{OH}$ in the same molecule with loss of water to make a cyclic ester.
walkthrough:
Spot the ester link forming**
The hydroxy acid $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ loses $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ between its own $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{OH}$ groups to give a five membered cyclic ester. Joining acid plus alcohol with loss of water is esterification, here intramolecular.
Final answer: esterification (intramolecular esterification / condensation)

hints: Compare the carbon skeletons of G and J, both $\text{C}_4$ aldehyde-alcohols, and see what is identical and what moves.
walkthrough:
See what moves and what stays**
Both G, $\text{OHCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, and J, $\text{OHCCH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, have the same functional groups, aldehyde plus alcohol, on the same four carbon chain. Only the position of the $\text{OH}$ group changes, from C4 to C3. That is positional isomerism.

hints: Look for the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)-}$ grouping, which gives a positive iodoform reaction, and check which of G or J contains it.
Recall the reagent is aqueous alkaline iodine, warmed, and the positive result is a yellow precipitate with antiseptic smell.
walkthrough:
Find the iodoform fingerprint**
Draw J out: $\text{OHC-CH}_2\text{-CH(OH)-CH}_3$. It ends in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)-}$. That group is oxidised by alkaline iodine to $\text{CH}_3\text{CO-}$ which then cleaves to yellow $\text{CHI}_3$. G has only $\text{HOCH}_2\text{-}$, a primary alcohol with no adjacent methyl, so it cannot do this.

State test and results clearly**
Warm each compound with $\text{I}_2\text{(aq)}$ in $\text{NaOH}$. G shows no change, the brown iodine colour remains. J gives a pale yellow precipitate of triiodomethane, $\text{CHI}_3$.
Final answer: test: add aqueous alkaline iodine ( $\text{I}_2$ in $\text{NaOH}$ ), warm; result with G: no change (stays brown); result with J: yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_3$

hints: Think about what $\text{NaBH}_4$ does to the $\text{CHO}$ group in G and J when they become diols.
walkthrough:
Follow the hydride**
$\text{NaBH}_4$ supplies hydride, $\text{H}^-$, to the carbonyl carbon of the aldehyde, converting $\text{-CHO}$ to $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$. Because it donates electrons (as hydride) and reduces the organic molecule, its role is reducing agent.
Final answer: reducing agent (reductant)

hints: Consider what happens when butane-1,4-diol and butane-1,3-diol each lose two molecules of water on hot $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.
walkthrough:
Dehydrate twice to the same diene**
Reduction gives $\text{HO(CH}_2)_4\text{?}$ actually $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ from G and $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ from J. Hot $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ removes $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from each alcohol to form $\text{C=C}$. Losing two waters from either $\text{C}_4$ diol leaves $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH-CH=CH}_2$, buta-1,3-diene.
Final answer: buta-1,3-diene, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH=CH}_2$

hints: Check P (carboxylic acid) and Q (ketone plus alcohol) for any $\text{C=C}$ bond that would decolourise bromine water.
Recall that 2,4-DNPH gives an orange precipitate only with aldehydes and ketones, not with carboxylic acids or alcohols.
Recall that aqueous sodium carbonate fizzes only with acids stronger than carbonic acid, such as carboxylic acids.
walkthrough:
Test for the alkene with bromine**
Neither P, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, nor Q, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH(OH)CH}_3$, has a $\text{C=C}$ bond. So $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$ stays orange in both cases, no decolourisation.

Test for the carbonyl with 2,4-DNPH**
2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine reacts with aldehydes and ketones to give an orange precipitate. P is a carboxylic acid, so no change. Q contains a ketone $\text{C=O}$, so orange precipitate forms.

Test for the acid with carbonate**
Aqueous $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ gives $\text{CO}_2$ effervescence with carboxylic acids: $2\text{RCOOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. P fizzes, Q (ketone plus secondary alcohol) shows no change.

Final answer: $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$: no change (stays orange) with P and no change (stays orange) with Q; 2,4-DNPH: no change with P and orange precipitate with Q; aqueous $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$: effervescence with P and no change with Q

hints: Use the wavenumbers, X near $1700\text{ cm}^{-1}$ and Z near $1050\text{ cm}^{-1}$, and the lactone structure of L to assign carbonyl and single bond stretches.
walkthrough:
Match peaks to the lactone**
L is a cyclic ester, so it must show a strong $\text{C=O}$ stretch around $1700\text{ cm}^{-1}$. That is peak X. It must also show $\text{C-O}$ single bond stretches around $1000$ to $1300\text{ cm}^{-1}$. That is peak Z.
Final answer: X is $\text{C=O}$ and Z is $\text{C-O}$

hints: Count the total carbons in $\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2)_4\text{COOH}$ including the $\text{COOH}$ carbon to give the systematic acid name.
walkthrough:
Count the longest acid chain**
$\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2)_4\text{COOH}$ has $5 + 1 = 6$ carbons with the $\text{COOH}$ carbon as C1. A six carbon straight chain acid is hexanoic acid.

hints: Add the atoms of the two cleavage products and subtract the oxygen atoms added during hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$ oxidation to find the formula of L.
walkthrough:
Rebuild R from the cleavage pieces**
Hot concentrated acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ in R to two $\text{COOH}$ groups. One piece is the lactone-$\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$) and the other is $\text{CH}_3\text{(CH}_2)_4\text{COOH}$ ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$). Joining them back by removing the added O atoms for the two new $\text{COOH}$ groups gives L as $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{20}\text{O}_2$, which fits a lactone with one $\text{C=C}$ in R.
